item.title: “She Will Be Quite a Manager”: From Plantation Owner to Girl Boss — Thu Sep 17, 5:30 PM — Ackland Art Museum
item.description: What do a Civil War-era plantation owner and a modern “girl boss” have in common? More than you think. Adelicia Acklen and Dorothy Thomas were two of the most powerful plantation-owning women—one in the US South and the other in South America—but both wielded the power of ownership by deploying and playing on particular ideas of femininity. This talk hosted by Carolina Public Humanities traces their unsettling legacy into the present, asking what happens when women gain power within systems built on inequality. Free, but space is limited; registration is required via the Carolina Public Humanities event webpage. About the speaker: Tanya Shields is an Associate Professor of Women’s and Gender Studies whose research focuses on Caribbean studies and plantation logics. She teaches courses on the Caribbean, the arts of activism, growing up girls globally, and the continuing influence of plantation economics and politics. item.title: When Are Polling Differences True Public Opinion Change? — Fri Sep 18, 10:00 AM — None
item.description:
September 18, 2026 (10:00 am-12:00 pm) Erin Hartman Associate Professor of Political Science University of California, Berkeley
Erin Hartman's research bridges statistics and the social sciences, developing methods that help researchers answer complex causal questions while strengthening collaboration across disciplines. Her work focuses on causal inference, survey design and analysis, external validity of experiments, falsification testing, and survey weighting.
Decomposing Changes Across Surveys
When different polls produce different results, how can we tell whether those differences reflect real changes in public opinion or simply differences in the surveys themselves?
In this talk, Hartman will present a formal framework for breaking down differences across surveys into three components: statistical noise, compositional differences, and true public opinion change.

item.title: A trifactor model for comparing retrospective and momentary assessments of emotions. — Fri Sep 18, 11:00 AM — None
item.description: It has long been known that different processes underlie momentary and retrospective reports of the same emotions. When answering retrospective questions about emotions, respondents rely on episodic memory and thus engage a variety of heuristics, leading to a so-called "memory-experience gap". The current study uses ecological momentary analysis (EMA) to systematically model the gaps between three types of measures of positive and negative emotions: momentary, daily retrospective, and weekly retrospective. Participants (N = 223) responded to momentary, daily retrospective, and weekly retrospective versions of the modified Differential Emotions Scale (mDES) of positive and negative affect for five weeks. item.title: CCN Colloquium: "Adaptive learning across development" — Fri Sep 18, 12:00 PM — LSRC - DIBS B035 Multipurpose Room
item.description:
In life's first two decades, children who know little about the world grow into young adults who harness rich knowledge of environmental structure to guide their behavior and accomplish their goals. In my talk, I will argue that the development of goal-directed behavior depends on learning to learn. I will present a series of studies examining how the computations and neural mechanisms that underlie value-guided memory, flexible reinforcement learning, and strategic exploration change from childhood to adulthood, and enable individuals to increasingly tailor their behaviors to the demands of varied environments across development.

item.description:
Speaker(s):
Prof. Jerry Reiter, Henry W. Newson Distinguished Professor of Statistical Science ('92 Mathematics):
Title: Is There a Future for Public Use Data?
Abstract: For decades, research and education in the social sciences have been facilitated by record-level, public use data files provided by statistical agencies and other data stewards. Today, however, the future of public use data is uncertain. The growth of readily available digital information and computational tools, while enormously beneficial for advancing research and education, has led to increased risks that ill-intentioned data users could mine the public use data to learn data subjects' identifies and sensitive information. I discuss the future of public use data in the social sciences, focusing on the risks to data subjects' privacy and confidentiality. item.title: Ethnomusicology Lecture: Yurika Tamura, UNC Chapel Hill — Fri Sep 18, 4:00 PM — Biddle Music Building
item.description:
What if Indigeneity is sound? This talk introduces Tamura's book project, Vibration of Others: Indigeneity as Sound and Sensation, in which she explores Ainu Indigeneity as sound and corporeal sensation.
The Ainu are Indigenous people of Japan. This simple statement took decades of activism to materialize: Japan officially acknowledged the Ainu as Indigenous people in 2019. Much of the success of Ainu activism is owing to the sounds and sensations they generated in the form of music performance. Ainu musicians and performance activists made their claims audible internationally, and in the process, they also produced a particular Ainu sonic philosophy on Indigeneity, covibrancy, and corporeal ethics.
This project articulates an Indigenous agent ontology specific to contemporary Ainu sounds and argues that Ainu sonic practices allow the Ainu to define Indigeneity in their own terms, contest Japanese ethnonationalism, and extend their ethical philosophy beyond their own politics of sove

item.title: Duke Arts Presents: Sacred Spaces — Fri Sep 18, 7:30 PM — Bryan Center Reynolds Industries Theater
item.description:
Few works in modern dance carry the legacy of Alvin Ailey's Revelations, a masterpiece set to spirituals and gospel music that has moved audiences worldwide since 1960 and remains the most widely seen work in modern dance history. In Sacred Spaces, Associate Artistic Director Matthew Rushing and Co-creator and Musical Director Du'Bois A'Keen revisit that legacy through a new lens.
Sacred Spaces expands on Sacred Places: Decoding the Spiritual, developed during Rushing and A'Keen's residency at Duke Divinity School this past April. The work originated from Rushing's vision to build a ballet around spirituals removed from Revelations when it was shortened for touring.
Sacred Spaces explores memory, community, and cultural inheritance. Performed by musicians, vocalists, dancers, and visual artists from across the Triangle, this new work honors the spirituality and communal spirit of Revelations while standing firmly on its own as a contemporary work.
Source: Duke University

item.title: Screen/Society--"About Face: Disrupting Ballet" (2025) w/ dir. Jennifer Lin | AADS Symposium — Sat Sep 19, 3:00 PM — Rubenstein Arts Center
item.description:
Special screening:
"About Face: Disrupting Ballet" (Jennifer Lin, 2025, 60 min, USA, English, DCP)
ABOUT FACE: DISRUPTING BALLET is a feature-length documentary that spotlights Georgina Pazcoguin and Phil Chan, two friends and NYC dancers of Asian descent, who are challenging ballet companies to rid The Nutcracker and other ballets of offensive racial stereotypes. What started as a pledge on a website has grown into a global movement, disrupting the elite world of ballet.
Gina, a soloist with the New York City Ballet, and Phil, an author, producer and choreographer, launch the global "Final Bow for Yellowface" movement [https://www.yellowface.org]. They post an online pledge and ask dancers to jettison offensive "yellowface" caricatures from ballets like The Nutcracker and La Bayadère. Hundreds from around the world sign the pledge.
We watch in real time as the Scottish Ballet updates its version of the Chinese dance to both high praise and stinging backlash.

item.description:
Celebrate the artistry, mentorship, and community at the heart of Duke Music during the 2026 Faculty & Student Gala Concert. This all-Mendelssohn program brings together distinguished faculty, accomplished alumni, and exceptional student musicians in honor of the retirement of renowned Mendelssohn scholar Dr. R. Larry Todd.
The program opens with the Duke Symphony Orchestra, conducted by Harry Davidson, performing the atmospheric Hebrides Overture, inspired by the dramatic Scottish landscape of Fingal's Cave. Next, pianist Bryan Tong joins the orchestra in a rare performance of Mendelssohn's unfinished Piano Concerto No. 3 in E Minor, meticulously reconstructed with the extraordinary musical scholarship and creativity of Dr. Todd.
The evening culminates with the Ciompi Quartet of Duke University and alumni musicians of the Larkspur Quartet in a performance of Mendelssohn's exhilarating Octet for Strings; a youthful masterpiece brimming with irrepressible energy.

item.title: Invasive Removal at Carol H. Johnson Environmental Education Park (Fuquay Varina) — Wed Sep 23, 9:00 AM
item.description:
Join NCWF South Wake Conservationists Chapter in partnership with Wake Audubon for an ongoing project to conserve and support the natural heritage of a unique nature park in Fuquay Varina. The NC Natural Heritage Progam lists portions of this site as 7 out of 10 for natural diversity, which is exceptional for a suburban/urban location! Last year we made a great start on removing invasive plants from the park. Now when someone pulls in they can see the creek from their parking spot, instead of a wall of privet and bradford pears! Not to mention the numerous fern, strawberry bushes and a multitude of other native plants we’ve freed up to grow. Volunteers will help cut or pull the invasives and haul them out by the parking lot. Fuquay Varina Public Works loads all this into large trailers and hauls it away as they are filled. Last time, we filled two trailers, and there is plenty more to go! REGISTER HERE
Source: NC Wildlife Federation

item.title: ‘United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today’ ADST Traveling Exhibition — Mon Sep 28, 7:30 AM — FedEx Global Education Center
item.description:
UNC Global Affairs is pleased to partner with the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training (ADST) to host a traveling exhibition on the history of American diplomacy, “United States Diplomacy: From Its Beginnings to Today.”
Created with support from the Una Chapman Cox Foundation, the 21-panel exhibition celebrates diplomatic accomplishments and traces diplomacy’s role across America’s 250-year history, from Benjamin Franklin’s mission to Paris during the Revolutionary War, to 21st-century challenges such as transnational terrorism, climate change and global health.
The exhibition begins during the opening reception for Diplomacy Week 2026 on Monday, Sept. 28, and will be on display in the FedEx Global Education Center until Friday, Oct. 2.

item.title: Play the Cyber Bowl — Thu Oct 1
item.description:
It's time to play the third annual Cyber Bowl, a month-long competition to determine which North Carolina university is the most cyber savvy.
All October long, students, faculty and staff can log into the Cyber Bowl website and take a short cybersecurity quiz. Each completed quiz earns a point for Carolina.
UNC-Chapel Hill faces off against nine other North Carolina universities with a lot to prove and two wins to defend. In the inaugural Cyber Bowl, Carolina won the championship by garnering the largest participation by percentage. Last year, Carolina fielded the most players — almost 2,000 — of any school.
The Cyber Bowl is sponsored by Information Technology Services and the Information Security Office as part of National Cybersecurity Awareness Month.
Source: UNC Chapel Hill

item.title: ‘Never A Bad Peace: Celebrating 250 Years of American Diplomacy’ with Adam Howard — Thu Oct 1, 5:30 PM — FedEx Global Education Center
item.description:
In 1783, Benjamin Franklin wrote, “May we never see another War! for in my Opinion there never was a good War, or a bad Peace.”
In this Diplomatic Discussion, the keynote lecture of Diplomacy Week 2026, Adam Howard, former chief historian at the U.S. Department of State, discusses three pivotal moments in American history shaped by the work of talented diplomats: the Revolutionary War, the Civil War and the aftermath of World War II.
Vice Provost for Global Affairs and Chief Global Officer Barbara Stephenson conducts a fireside chat, followed by questions from students in the audience. Afterwards, join Howard and Stephenson in the Florence and James Peacock Atrium for pizza and discussion.

item.title: AI Security Non-Neogtiables with Joyce Rancani — Mon Oct 5, 1:00 PM
item.description:
On Oct. 5 at 1 p.m., join a virtual event with Joyce Rancani, chief technology security officer at Qualys, an industry-leading enterprise cyber risk and security platform.
In her presentation, “AI Security Non-Negotiables,” Rancani will discuss how as enterprise adoption accelerates from static chatbots to autonomous, action-taking AI agents, the attack surface expands into non-deterministic execution paths, prompt-driven exploitation and complex supply chain vulnerabilities.
Her session will break down the non-negotiables of securing autonomous systems across their entire lifecycle from the "brilliant basics" of zero trust identity and runtime blast-radius containment, to the rigorous principles of securely designing, building, deploying and continuously monitoring AI agents in production.
The event is free to join and does not require registration. Students seeking campus life experience (CLE) credit should RSVP for the event in Heel Life to receive credit.

item.title: Remembering & Resisting: LGBTQ+ History From Nazi Germany to Today — Mon Oct 5, 4:00 PM — Gregg Museum of Art & Design
item.description:
Join us at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design for the opening of the exhibition Remembering & Resisting: LGBTQ+ History From Nazi Germany to Today and a keynote address by curator Jake Newsome, founder of The Pink Triangle Legacies Project. Newsome's keynote address, "Enemies of the State: The Nazi Persecution of LGBTQ+ People," will examine the complex motivations behind Nazi leaders' choice to persecute LGBTQ+ people and to present it as vital to the success of the Third Reich. A Q&A and a book signing will follow the presentation. Please register to attend.
Remembering & Resisting: LGBTQ+ History From Nazi Germany to Today is a traveling exhibit that explores the persecution of queer and trans people under Nazi rule and the long, ongoing struggle to reclaim their histories. Beginning in Weimar Germany’s early LGBTQ+ movements, the exhibit traces how the Nazi regime targeted those deemed “undesirable” and how survivors faced continued criminalization and silence long after 1945. item.description:
Durham Geeks We meet at Moon Dog Meadery under Joe Van Gogh on Broad Street every Monday night. We have loads of games (some belong to MoonDog, some are brought by attendees), a fun and welcoming group of folks (always eager to have more, however!), and there are always folks eager to teach games to those who haven't played certain titles.
Moondog has a growing collection of canned and bottled brews, ciders, and colas in addition to their in-house-brewed meads. There are also some snacks like chips and popcorn. Sometimes, folks bring in other treats to share. If you do, please mark them as containing any common allergens.
Outside food (delivered, brought in, or homemade) is welcomed and encouraged. Outside drinks are not.
